texts: Recap: Our Research Plan
Attention allocation and navigation information design for newcomers to Hong Kong
RESEARCH QUESTION
How can navigation information be classified by its associated interaction burdens to improve when and how it is delivered?
01  Field observation
Record visible actions and information use during natural navigation.
02  Interviews
Use semi-structured interviews to understand participants’ decisions.
03  Analysis
Connect observation and accounts for later qualitative analysis.
Route Candidates
PolyU South Gate vicinity → K11 Art Mall
13 min / 900 m

Chatham Road South
Granville + Carnarvon Roads
Hanoi Road
PolyU South Gate vicinity → Temple entrance (Kwun Yum Temple)
20 min / 1.3 km

Chatham Road North
Hung Hom residential streets
Station Lane
PolyU South Gate vicinity → Clock Tower
24 min / 1.7 km

Chatham + Granville Roads
Nathan + Hankow Roads
Salisbury Road to forecourt
Why This Route? Participant Familiarity
Participant-related reason: a route and destinations unfamiliar to all five participants
participants were unfamiliar with the route and destinations
01 Unfamiliar route
They did not already know how to reach the destinations.
02 No previous K11 visits
None of the five had been to K11 before the study.
03 No previous store visits
None had visited the target Barbour store.
WHY THIS MATTERS
The setting supports observing how people seek and use navigation information in an unfamiliar place.
Why This Route? Environmental Conditions
Route-related reason: varied street conditions and an indoor destination
PolyU South Gate (Outdoor start) → K11 Art Mall (Required waypoint) → K11 MUSEA · Barbour (Indoor endpoint · 3F, Shop 319)
01  Dense commercial surroundings
Tsim Sha Tsui combines pedestrian activity, commercial frontages and many competing sources of information.
02  Varied street network
Wide main roads, narrow lanes, multiple junctions and blocks create opportunities for route and turn confirmation.
03  Building landmarks
Prominent buildings such as K11 provide potential references for orientation and destination recognition.
04  Multilevel and indoor wayfinding
The district includes multilevel pedestrian spaces. Finding Barbour adds floor, directory and shop-location decisions.
These are route-selection considerations. The actual features encountered must be checked against each participant’s records.
Warm-up: Preparing for Natural Navigation
A campus practice session before the formal route
Site A: Library podium forecourt → Site B: University / Suen Chi Sun squares → Site C: Innovation Tower forecourt (Core V)
Navigate as usual
Use apps naturally, switch apps, and ask passers-by when needed. No continuous explanation is required.
Become familiar with the process
Participants and researchers practise the recording procedure. The warm-up does not rehearse the formal route.
Campus A → B → C practice records remain separate from the main navigation task.
Fieldwork Workflow: From Walking to Interview
Capture the walk, build observation logs, then revisit selected moments
DURING THE WALK
Participant: Navigates naturally with a microphone to capture spontaneous speech.
Researcher: Records video and makes voice memos of observed actions and context.
01  Transcribe and review
Transcribe the researcher’s voice memos, manually check the text, and organise observation logs.
02  Interview with video support
Use selected clips and logged events in semi-structured interviews to discuss decisions and information use.
RECORD: Walk + audio + video ↓ ORGANISE: Reviewed observation logs ↓ REVISIT: Participant explanations
Researcher voice memos are fieldnotes. They are not participant think-aloud data.
Data Collection Progress
Field observations are complete; interviews and organisation are still in progress
5 navigation observations completed
2 participant interviews still to complete
Video recordings: Walking context and later verification
Observation logs: Field observations organised from notes
GPS tracks: Supporting route and location context
Interview records: Participant explanations; collection ongoing
Some materials have undergone initial organisation; the full dataset is not yet ready for analysis.
Initial Data Organisation
Descriptive action tags for observation logs — not yet the qualitative codebook
S  STOP  Visible halt in stepping
P  PHONE_VIEW  Discernible viewing toward the phone
I  PHONE_INPUT  Visible phone touch, swipe or input
H  HEAD_TURN  Visible change in head direction
G  SIGN_VIEW  Viewing an identifiable sign
Q  HELP_REQUEST  Audible or reliably documented request
R  RESEARCHER_PROMPT  Researcher instruction or intervention
T  RESEARCHER_TALK
Talking with the researcher; unclear content is marked T?.
K  KIOSK_USE
Viewing or typing on a public electronic directory; not coded as I.
T and K: working codes added during fieldwork, unified across all five cases.
Q is not inferred from a backward look or showing a phone. R is a researcher prompt; T is conversation with the researcher.
Data Filtering: Video Memo Coding
Re-describing observed segments from voice-memo logs, checked against video and interviews
HOW SEGMENTS WERE FILTERED
01 Voice-memo observation logs
Start from the researcher’s transcribed voice memos: the observation log of each walk.
02 Check against the video
Review each logged moment in the recording; confirm, correct or add what the memo missed.
03 Corroborate with interviews
Use semi-structured interview accounts to support or question the segment, where available.
04 Re-describe with code combinations
Rewrite each selected segment as a code sequence, e.g. S + P → S + H, with location, situation and environment.
FILTERED RECORDS BY PARTICIPANT
Participant | Main video | Filtered records | ★ / ◆ / ○
P01  Sarah | 37:38 | 36 segments | 19 / 17 / –
P02  Caicai | 35:13 | 36 segments | 19 / 15 / 2
P03  Peter | multiple clips | 70 timed records | v2, not graded
P05  Chenggong | 30:44 | 34 segments | 19 / 11 / 4
★ key segment   ◆ supporting / smooth contrast   ○ context.  Grades mark filtering use, not burden severity.
Segments are review windows for later coding, not counts of independent events; no rates are derived from them.
Data Case: A Re-routed Back Lane
One filtered segment from P04 (Tom), read from observation to participant account
LOCATION: Hau Fook Street lane → right turn into a back service lane
SITUATION: Google Maps re-routed him into the back lane
ENVIRONMENT: Narrow and cluttered, workers on site; no general pedestrians, street names or signs
CODE  |  OBSERVED IN VIDEO  (v = seconds in file)
H  v650–660  Follows a passer-by into the narrow lane
P  v661  Views the screen while turning right
P  v690–699  Frequent screen checks while watching the workers
S + I  v705–712  Stops by a shutter; zooms the map with both hands (~8 s)
VOICE MEMO CROSS-CHECK: “Unsure whether this is the lane; keeps checking Google Maps and looking back” — confirmed by video. A memo “pause” is not visible in the continuous video: to verify.
PARTICIPANT ACCOUNT: On-site interview: the lane was the most stressful part — “honestly, a bit scary”, “not like a proper road”. He linked it to an earlier wrong step that made Google Maps re-route.
STATUS: Checked against video  ·  high priority
Quotes are translated from Chinese. Observation, cross-checks and participant account stay in separate fields; interpretation is written last.
Voice Memos Checked Against Video
Video review confirms, corrects and adds to the researchers’ fieldnotes
CONFIRMED
P04 · V02 — Memo: “keeps checking the phone for direction” on a straight road. Video: about 17 s of continuous screen viewing.
P01 · M01–M40 — Phone checks at crossings, restart after the waypoint, missed entrance and turn-back, floor search: the sequence matches.
P05 · V30–V33 — Reports location drift, then relies on overhead shop signs; the Barbour / 319 sign appears in frame.
CORRECTED
P04 · V15 — Memo: phone use rose at a crowded crossing. Video: phone viewing at its lowest (15%); attention on crowd and signals.
P05 · V19–V21 — Memo’s “Art Mall entrance” was outside K11 MUSEA; the phone at 23:03 reads K11 MUSEA.
P01 · M03–M04 — Some phone views were read as social media; the screen is not legible, so the purpose stays unknown.
ADDED
P04 · V24 — In the tunnel, sign viewing and phone viewing alternate three times.
P02 · v1732–1772 — Keyboard and search list visible: a re-search, plus an app switch in the second file.
P01 · P05 — Researcher help logged by type: rule clarification, direction, target reminder, permission to switch apps.
Holding a phone is not viewing it: P is coded only from visible gaze. Voice memos stay fieldnotes, checked against video.
Possible Findings So Far
Candidate patterns from the filtered segments — to be tested in cross-case analysis
01 At the waypoint, the hand-over to the next leg is unclear | appears: P01 P02 P04 P05 | P01 V14–15 · P04 V16 · P05 V10
02 Underground crossings call for extra checking of map and signs | appears: P01 P03 P04 P05 | P01 V18–21 · P04 V22–24 · P05 V13–17
03 Seeing the target building does not show the way in | appears: P01 P04 P05 | P01 V25 · P04 V21, V26–27 · P05 V19–21
04 Indoors, floor and shop finding draws on extra sources: kiosks, directories, shop signs, other apps | appears: P01 P02 P03 P04 P05 | P03 V24, V47–55 · P04 V29–31 · P05 V21–25
05 The phone is often held low while walking; checks cluster around junctions and stops | appears: P01 P02 P04 P05 | P04 V03–05 · P05 V01–12 · P02 QC01
● appears in filtered segments   ○ not yet identified — not evidence of absence
From single-case filtering only: no burden levels or frequencies yet. Patterns enter the qualitative codebook after cross-case checking.
Data Processing
Prepare traceable information-interaction events for later qualitative analysis
PRIMARY: Observation logs — Build the event record
VERIFY: Video — Check actions and timing
CONTEXT: GPS — Support location and route
Observation: What was seen or reliably recorded? Action, time, place and information source.
Participant Account: What did the participant say? Link the explanation to the relevant moment.
Interpretation: What might the evidence mean? Keep the inference and its support explicit.
EVENT RECORD   =   context + information source + action sequence + linked account
Challenges and Adjustments
Make the record more usable without claiming more than the evidence supports
01 Writing while walking is difficult → Use researcher voice memos, then organise them into observation logs.
02 Transcription needs checking → Manually review transcripts and uncertain passages; use video for verification.
03 Kiosk use and researcher talk add actions → Unify them as T and K, then back-check earlier records (G* / D* → K).
04 Behaviour does not explain its own meaning → Do not infer being lost or burdened from stopping or looking at a phone alone.
Next Steps
Complete the evidence before moving into qualitative analysis
01 Complete the two remaining interviews →
02 Align observations with participant accounts →
03 Check whether the evidence is sufficient
EVIDENCE SUFFICIENT?
YES  →  Begin qualitative analysis
Build the qualitative codebook; conduct within-case and cross-case analysis.
NO  →  Recruit one more participant
Recruit one eligible participant and repeat the observation and interview workflow.
